etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English nauther, from nother. Cognate with neither. By surface analysis, not +‎ or.

definitions.definition: (literary) And... not (introducing a negative statement, without necessarily following one).

quote.citation: 1797, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner:
quote.text: Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink.
And, moreover, I had made my vow to preserve my rank unknown till the crusade should be accomplished; nor did I mention it  […]

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXXV, page 54:
quote.text: The cheeks drop in; the body bows;Man dies: nor is there hope in dust:  […]

definitions.definition: A function word introducing each except the first term of a series, indicating none of them is true.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: I love your majesty / According to my bond, nor more nor less.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book IV”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: But neither breath of Morn when she ascends / With charm of earliest birds; nor rising sun / On this delightful land, nor herb, fruit, flower, / Glistering with dew; nor fragrance after showers; / Nor grateful Evening mild; nor silent Night / With this her solemn bird; nor walk by moon, / Or glittering starlight, without thee is sweet.

quote.citation: 2013 June 22, “T time”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8841, page 68:
quote.text: The ability to shift profits to low-tax countries by locating intellectual property in them […] is often assumed to be the preserve of high-tech companies. […] current tax rules make it easy for all sorts of firms to generate […] “stateless income”: profit subject to tax in a jurisdiction that is neither the location of the factors of production that generate the income nor where the parent firm is domiciled.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: I love your majesty / According to my bond, nor more nor less.

quote.citation: 1601, Ben Jonson, Poetaster or The Arraignment: […], London:  […]  [R. Bradock] for M[atthew] L[ownes] […], published 1602, →OCLC, Act I, scene ii:
quote.text: Nor you nor your house were so much as spoken of before I disbased myself.

definitions.definition: Used to introduce a further negative statement.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter I, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: I was about to say that I had known the Celebrity from the time he wore kilts. But I see I will have to amend that, because he was not a celebrity then, nor, indeed, did he achieve fame until some time after I left New York for the West.

quote.citation: 1861, George Eliot, Silas Marner, London: Penguin Books, published 1967, page 131:
quote.text: 'I used to think, when you first come into these parts, as you were no better nor you should be.'

quote.citation: 1967, Barbara Sleigh, Jessamy, Sevenoaks, Kent: Bloomsbury, published 1993, →ISBN, page 92:
quote.text: I wouldn’t like to live here though, not after dark. Sooner you nor me.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Etymology 1 (sense 2 above), reinterpreted as not + or or negation + or.
